issues.legal_issue: A breach of a non-statutory employment restriction does not, on the evidence in this case, bar recovery of property owned by the employee.
material_facts: The employee’s service rules were not produced in evidence and were not shown to be statutory.
The rules prohibited carrying on a business as its owner but did not prohibit acting as another person’s manager or agent.
The business was held out as belonging to another person while the employee was employed.
issues.conclusion: The arrangement was not shown to be unlawful on the basis of the service rules, and the employee was not barred from seeking recovery of the business on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: The appellate court held, and the Supreme Court did not disturb, that a breach or attempted evasion of rules not shown to be statutory does not necessarily make an arrangement illegal; the rules themselves were not in evidence, and carrying on business as a manager or agent was permitted.

predicates.ownership_recovery_case: A person seeks recovery of a business on the basis that the person owns it.
predicates.employment_restriction_not_shown_statuto: The employment restriction relied on to challenge the arrangement is not shown to be statutory.
predicates.business_as_agent_permitted: The restriction permits the employee to conduct the business as another person’s manager or agent.

issues.definition: When a person seeks recovery of an owned business and the employment restriction is not shown to be statutory while permitting the person to act as an agent, recovery is not barred by that restriction.

issues.legal_issue: A later tax evasion connected with a benami arrangement does not bar an owner’s title-based recovery when evasion of tax was not the arrangement’s original object and recovery does not require enforcement of an unlawful transaction.
material_facts: The lower courts found that the plaintiff supplied the funds for the business and was its true owner, while the defendant was held out as its nominal owner to circumvent employment rules.
The plaintiff later submitted false information to the tax authorities, causing his personal income to escape taxation and the business income to be assessed at a lower rate.
The courts found that evading tax was not the purpose of the arrangement when it was made.
The plaintiff had entrusted management and possession of the business to the defendant for return, and the defendant refused to return it when requested.
issues.conclusion: The tax evasion did not make the arrangement on which the plaintiff’s claim rested unlawful; the plaintiff could enforce his title and recover possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, an agreement is unlawful if its object is forbidden by law or would defeat the provisions of law. The majority distinguished a claim that must rely on an unlawful transaction from a claim to enforce title where the unlawful transaction is not integral to the claim. It referred to A.R.P.L. Palanianna Chettiar v. P.L.A.R. Arunasalam Chettiar as an example of a claim requiring reliance on fraud against public administration, and Sajan Singh v. Sardara Ali as an example of relief on an independent possessory basis. The majority found no original tax-evasion object and did not need to decide the broader distinction in cases where an unlawful purpose had been established.

rule.if: ownership_recovery_case and beneficial_ownership_proved and later_tax_evasion_occurred and revenue_evasion_not_original_object and business_entrusted_for_return and holder_refused_return

predicates.ownership_recovery_case: A person seeks recovery of a business on the basis of ownership.
predicates.beneficial_ownership_proved: The evidence establishes that the claimant, rather than the nominal holder, beneficially owned the business.
predicates.later_tax_evasion_occurred: After the arrangement was made, the claimant used false information in tax dealings and obtained a tax advantage.
predicates.revenue_evasion_not_original_object: The arrangement was not made for the purpose of evading tax.
predicates.business_entrusted_for_return: The claimant entrusted the business to the holder on the understanding that it would be returned.
predicates.holder_refused_return: The holder refused to return the business when the claimant demanded it.

issues.definition: If beneficial ownership is proved and a business entrusted for return is withheld, later tax evasion does not prevent the owner from recovering it when tax evasion was not the arrangement’s original object.

issues.legal_issue: A person who had possession of property may recover it on an independent possessory claim even if the original acquisition was an illegal benami transaction.
material_facts: The plaintiff was in physical possession of the property before leaving for medical reasons.
He put the defendant in possession on the understanding that possession and management would be returned when he came back.
The plaintiff returned and sought possession, but the defendant refused.
The lower courts found these facts proved.
issues.conclusion: In Justice Ayyangar’s separate opinion, the plaintiff’s claim based on prior possession and the defendant’s refusal to return the property was independent of, and not tainted by, the allegedly illegal original purchase; that claim supported dismissal of the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Justice Ayyangar applied the distinction between enforcing an illegal transaction and asserting an independent right to possession. He relied on Sajan Singh v. Sardara Ali, where recovery was allowed on a possessory claim independent of the unlawful acquisition, and discussed Bowmakers v. Barnet Instruments in considering whether a claimant must rely on the illegal transaction. He also referred to section 23 of the Indian Contract Act and the principle in Petherpermal Chetty v. Muniandi Servai that a claimant may be denied relief where an unlawful purpose has been achieved and recovery depends on asserting the tainted title. The majority dismissed the appeal on its own reasoning that the original tax-evasion purpose was not proved.

rule.if: possessory_recovery_case and prior_possession_proved and possession_entrusted_for_conditional_return and holder_refused_return and claim_independent_of_illegal_acquisition

predicates.possessory_recovery_case: A claimant seeks recovery of property on the basis of prior possession rather than solely on title arising from its acquisition.
predicates.prior_possession_proved: The claimant was in possession before the other person obtained possession.
predicates.possession_entrusted_for_conditional_ret: The claimant placed the other person in possession on the understanding that the property would be returned.
predicates.holder_refused_return: The person holding the property refused to return it when asked.
predicates.claim_independent_of_illegal_acquisition: The claimant can establish the possessory claim without relying on the allegedly illegal acquisition.

issues.definition: A claimant who previously possessed property may recover it when possession was entrusted for return and the holder refuses, if the claim is independent of the allegedly illegal acquisition.
